nh_eagle_mtn_cliff_jackson.blurb: A small hillside crag above Jackson village, tucked in the trees behind a historic hotel. Roughly half sport and half trad, the routes begin at easy 5.4 ground but the bulk sit between 5.9 and 5.12, with a few 5.13 lines for strong climbers. The wall drops into shade early, which makes it a good pick for hot summer afternoons. The cleaning is recent and some loose rock can still turn up, so wear a helmet and test your holds. It pairs well with a day at nearby Jackson Crag, and the short walk keeps it easy to fit in around other plans.

nh_3_amphitheater_area.blurb: The busiest section of Frankenstein Cliff in Crawford Notch, and one of the nearest to the road. It is a winter ice venue: most of the lines are water ice, with a handful of mixed pitches, and the grades run from a gentle WI1 up to WI5 with the bulk at WI3 and WI4. Mixed routes range from M5 to M7. Many lines are one or two pitches, which suits climbers building ice skills, and top-rope setups are easy to arrange. The cliff stays cold and shaded, so layer up for belays. Check the lines from a distance before committing.

nh_hatchet_area.blurb: A quiet cluster of large boulders in the Upper Black Jacks zone of Rumney, close to the better-known Black Jacks but visited far less. Every problem here is a boulder problem, and the spread is wide: easy slabs at V0, a solid core of V2 to V4, then steeper compression problems in the V6 and V7 range, topped by one very hard sit start. Some lines are tall and the landings can be uncomfortable, so bring several pads and a spotter. The walk in crosses slabby ground and weaves through the trees, so it feels a bit remote.

nh_the_central_wall.blurb: The broad middle section of Cathedral Ledge, the big granite cliff above North Conway. Mostly long trad lines that follow corners and cracks, some well over 400 feet, with most free climbing between 5.10 and 5.12 and a few easier or harder outliers. Several lines are aid climbs, up to serious grades, and two are bolted. Good lines get modest traffic, so expect some dirt and moss, and at least one chimney can be wet and thinly protected. The usual finish is walking off the top or a double-rope rappel. A route for experienced parties comfortable with committing terrain.

nh_exeter_boulder_the.blurb: A single large granite block standing on its own near the Rinks at Exeter, in the seacoast part of New Hampshire. Problems cover all four faces, and there are about two dozen with variations. The grades start at V0 and are friendly to beginners, with most lines in the V0 to V4 range, then a few harder problems up to V7 and one much harder outlier. A tall unclimbed prow is still a project. It is part of the larger Exeter forest bouldering scene, so it makes a handy quick stop, though bugs can be fierce in warm months.

nh_mount_oscar.blurb: A semi-secluded cliff in the Zealand Valley of the White Mountains, mostly traditional routes with a few bolted lines and some top-rope options. Rock is fairly clean, and bolts are placed where cracks run out. Climbs run from easy fifth class through the 5.8 and 5.9 range, with a handful of 5.11 testpieces, and the ratings are known to feel stiff. The base sits in shade and the approach is short, which makes it a nice summer day out. The setting is quiet compared with the busier North Conway cliffs.

nh_the_cathedral_cave.blurb: A steep, bolted pocket at the foot of Cathedral Ledge near North Conway, sitting between the Mordor Wall and the Central Wall. This is the cliff's hard sport zone: almost all of the sport lines are 5.12 and 5.13, with a few reaching 5.14, plus a few short aid lines. Its reputation is for chipped and sometimes loose rock, yet some routes are worthwhile. It works as a quick upper-body session after a day on the nearby trad lines. The routes stay dry in light rain but seep after long wet spells.

nh_ricochet_boulder_the.blurb: A large boulder in Rumney's Moat Boulders zone, immediately west of the huge Moat Boulder. It is still being developed, with about two dozen problems spread widely in difficulty: a few at V1 to V3, a middle group around V4 and V5, then a run of V7 and V8 lines and a couple of V10 to V12 testpieces. The moat of the name is a seasonal stream bed that tends to surround the blocks. Climbers have built log and branch platforms for crash pads, so the ground can be uneven. A solid choice for strong boulderers.
